source.title: Unified Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Ethan Caballero; P. Jaini; David Krueger; Irina Rish

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits and compares alternative scaling-law forms on reported scaling datasets, then evaluates extrapolation on held-out points. This is a conceptual test of scaling-law predictability, not a direct reproduction of the original experiments.
record.gate_note: The empirical language results reuse datasets from earlier work; those source studies' results are not separately counted as this paper's experiments. The paper reports RMSLE comparisons for fitted forms and explicit figure-based extrapolation claims. Its method for deriving compute-optimal input values is presented, but no resulting compute-optimal parameter/token trend is reported. Width/depth results vary both together and do not compare architectures at fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: The study refits prior scaling datasets, including Hoffmann et al.'s Chinchilla data, Muennighoff et al.'s repeated-data runs, LLaMA/HGRN2 runs and ViT/JFT runs. It compares held-out extrapolation RMSLE of the standard power-law forms (CF, DC) against a broken multivariate form (UNSL). This is a results-based argument that single power-law forms extrapolate worse and need restating. It is not a reproduction of the original experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right; correct it. UNSL is the best extrapolator on 88.89% of language tasks and 60.87% of vision tasks, not on all tasks. It beats CF/DC and the ablations on the reused datasets. The authors also state that extrapolating past a hyperbreak requires fit points near it.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits a new multivariate broken scaling-law form and ablations to previously reported scaling datasets; it is not a reproduction of Kaplan et al. or Hoffmann et al.'s experiments. It compares against CF and related functional forms and includes analysis of sourced language scaling data.
record.method_sensitivity: Extrapolation accuracy changes with the functional form and its additive-symmetry components. Fit selection includes validation-based choices of break counts and regularization; the authors also caution that extrapolation across a hyperbreak depends on the distance from fitting points to that break.

fits_no_version.finding: UNSL extrapolates test-time scaling of MAA 2024 error vs chain-of-thought length (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time compute scaling follows a predictable (broken) scaling law.

fits_no_version.finding: On an MNIST-1D MLP, nonmonotonic scaling in learning rate, init std and steps is fit better by UNSL than by an equal-parameter ablation (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hyperparameter-dependent nonmonotonic scaling can be modelled by additive-symmetry terms.

record.problems: Language and vision scaling datasets are taken from prior work rather than newly trained models in this study. Most numerical findings are comparative RMSLE values for fitted functions, not direct tests of individual power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation. Some additional extrapolation results are figure-only. The authors note that adequate proximity of fit points to each hyperbreak is needed for reliable extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 A1 and A2 scores were omitted; the CF and UNSL results were retained to keep the comparison focused on the standard scaling form and the paper's proposed form. Table 2 A1, A2, and A3 scores were omitted; DC and UNSL results were retained as the baseline-versus-proposed-form comparison. Table 3's 21 separate bivariate vision task/model results and Figures 15-16 (width/depth and batch-size examples) were omitted because they do not add a direct test of the selected claim versions beyond the retained aggregate vision and modality examples. Table 1's percentage-of-tasks-best summary is omitted as a summary of comparisons already represented in rows.

untested.parts: No single-variable power-law fits or exponents for loss with other factors non-bottlenecked.

Held-out points are only those above half the max of each input, about a 2x extrapolation. Orders-of-magnitude extrapolation is not tested for language; Appendix 14 does so only for a sparse-parity MLP.
Appendix 12 gives a Lagrangian method only; no compute-optimal N/D trends are reported.
Width and depth are varied together for an MLP (Fig. 15), with no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Video, fine-tuning and transfer are untested; repeated data appears only via the r1 trivariate fit; RL is figure-only.
Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss is not tested.
Effects of parameter counting and data choice on exponents, and disagreement in the compute-optimal split, are not tested.

missing.what: Limit of predictability: extrapolating past a hyperbreak requires fit points close to it (sparse-parity MLP).
Extrapolation an order of magnitude larger in several dimensions at once (sparse-parity MLP), figure only.

record.verdict_notes: All data are reused from prior work. The 'Chinchilla' rows are Hoffmann et al.'s own runs, obtained by correspondence; the study is not itself an original source. The extrapolation gap is only about 2x (held out = above half of each input's max), so V2's orders-of-magnitude claim is barely probed. Rows comparing UNSL with its own ablations (A1-A3, Table 6) are method-variant comparisons and are unlinked. V2 was removed from downstream and vision rows because V2 concerns language pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not directly test whether held-out pretraining cross-entropy follows a power law in an individual variable when the other variables are not bottlenecks, or report fitted exponents for that test.
Does not establish prediction across all model scales or for all language-model setups; tests held-out extrapolation on the datasets described.
Although Appendix 12 gives equations for deriving compute-optimal inputs from a fitted UNSL, no measured compute-optimal parameter/token allocations or growth exponents are reported.
Width and depth are varied simultaneously in a figure, not compared at fixed parameter count; no test of small architecture effects at fixed size.

Reports extrapolation results in vision and reinforcement learning, and a figure for inference scaling; does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer, and does not establish that a single ordinary power-law form applies in these settings.
Tests extrapolation of downstream task metrics, including CSR and LAMBADA; does not test whether downstream performance is predictable specifically from pretraining loss.

Shows that the choice of functional form/additive symmetries affects fit and extrapolation accuracy. Does not test disagreement in published exponents due to parameter counting, data choices, or compute-optimal allocation trends.
